stories.headline: Khelo India Sports Goods Manufacturing Scheme
stories.title: Khelo India Sports Goods Manufacturing Scheme
stories.summary: On October 28, the Union Cabinet approved the Khelo India Sports Goods Manufacturing Scheme with an outlay of INR 1,856.67 crore. The money will be spent from 2027 to 2034. This scheme was first announced in the Union Budget along with a timeline that matters, as often we have seen good ideas often stay on paper only. Currently, India produces a lot of sports goods. A case in point is Jalandhar and Meerut. The two big centres are popular for making sports items and products. Together the two cities have over 250 exporting units and nearly 20,000 household units. About 90% of production comes from small and micro firms. Especially the bat manufacturing industry is massive, India producers are experts in the field. Indian brands and makers hold about 75% to 80% of the global cricket bat market. But our equipment exports are only $275 million. The world exports about $52 billion. That gap is massive. Smaller firms find it hard to expand. As per the provision of this scheme they lack testing labs, design help and obviously financial assistance. They also struggle to get the certificates that foreign buyers ask for. How will the scheme work? The scheme will probably work on multiple fronts (six-stages). On the first level, it plans manufacturing zones. These will bring makers, suppliers, testing labs and design centres to one place. There may be four such zones, each over 300 acres. While on the second stage it offers money for investment. Anchor investors who put in at least INR 100 crore get 20% support on capital spending. Makers who invest INR 10 crore or more can get up to 15% as turnover-linked support. Together, these two parts have INR 1,130 crore. In the third stage, it helps in holding up existing clusters that are already on the ground. Shared facilities will be upgraded, with costs split with the States. This is where small firms stand to gain most. In the fourth stage, it pays for certification. INR 105 crore is set aside. The government will cover 70% of the cost of a first certificate and 50% of renewals. A bat or a helmet with an international seal sells more easily abroad. It backs new ideas on the fifth vertical. Centres of Excellence will study materials and protective gear. Start-ups registered with DPIIT can get grants of up to INR 20 lakh. On the sixth level, which is the outreach stage, it covers skills and marketing. There will be training, an India Sports Expo and a Brand India campaign. Relying on other schemes Khelo India Sports Goods Manufacturing Scheme will take assistance from other schemes. For instance the zones will use land and sheds from the BHAVYA scheme and NICDC industrial parks. Research will link with the Anusandhan National Research Foundation. Marketing will use the Export Promotion Mission. This is termed to be a very sensible and useful measure. The government is not building everything new. It is patching the gaps from the already existing design. The design will not only give cash to the beneficiaries but will fix the whole chain, from factory to certificate to buyer. However, there remains some pertinent questions. For example, large investors will gain from the 20% support. Will small firms see the same benefit? Nearly 90% of the sector is small, so the scheme must reach them. The cluster upgrades will decide that. Land acquisition will be another test to determine the positive outcome. Zones of 300 acres need clearances and State cooperation. If there are any delays there it means it will slow down everything. Besides, what matters more is the timing. As we know Los Angeles will be hosting the Olympics in 2028. Ahmedabad is also going to host the Commonwealth Games in 2030. Brisbane follows in 2032. So there is every possibility that the demand for equipment will rise in the coming years. What authorities are trying to gain out of this scheme, is that it wants India to make more of its own sports goods and import less. It wants more exports, more jobs and better quality. As per the official estimation predictions, the exports could reach $8.1 billion by 2036 which implies as many as 54 lakh jobs. That is a big leap if executed well. Furthermore, this scheme has been made to develop a strong relationship between sport and industry. As Khelo India builds players. This scheme is going to build the equipment they use. If both work, an Indian athlete may one day train, and win, with gear made in Jalandhar or Meerut. That is the ultimate goal of Khelo India Sports Goods Manufacturing Scheme. (COURTESY: PIB SRINAGAR)

stories.headline: Kashmir's Decreasing Snowfall Signals Alarming Link to Global Warming
stories.title: Kashmir's Decreasing Snowfall Signals Alarming Link to Global Warming
stories.summary: Kashmir is facing a crisis as its snowfall declines. This reduction affects not just the landscape but also the people and the environment. Recent studies show a strong link between decreasing snowfall in Kashmir and global warming. As the region experiences unusual winter weather, experts warn that the effects go beyond just beautiful scenery. This trend highlights the urgent need for global climate action. For generations, Chillai Kalan, a harsh 40-day winter, shaped life in the Kashmir Valley. It usually brought a thick layer of snow that acted as a natural reservoir, protecting the region's delicate ecosystem. Recent winters look very different. Snowfall is decreasing and arriving later, so it can't properly fill the glaciers or recharge groundwater. This change affects more than just Kashmir's famous winter beauty; it highlights a growing climate crisis. With less snow, the valley faces serious risks to its water supply and farming economy. Fewer snowflakes mean less water for rivers and crops. Recent studies indicate that snowfall has declined by more than 30% over the past two decades, raising alarm among environmental scientists and residents alike. With snow serving as a vital water source for agriculture and hydropower, the implications of this shift are profound and far-reaching. Local farmers are reporting lower crop yields, worsening food shortages in a region already facing high unemployment and limited resources. As temperatures rise and snowfall decreases, habitats face serious stress, which could lead to extinctions and ecosystem changes. The tourism-based economy of Kashmir, which relies on winter sports and beautiful scenery, is also at risk, threatening jobs and local businesses. Why Kashmir's Flood Red Flags Went Unheard Kashmir’s floods are usually called natural disasters. However, the reality is more troubling: the floods have become administrative failures caused by neglect and poor policies. Years ago, engineers and experts warned that Srinagar was heading for a flood disaster. Er. Ghulam Nabi Mirti wrote an important article called “Fighting Floods Fury in Kashmir” on September 29, 2006, in the local newspaper. He detailed how illegal constructions, silt buildup in the River Jhelum, shrinking wetlands, and uncontrolled urban growth were putting Srinagar at risk. The article highlighted vulnerable areas such as Lasjan, Padshahibagh, Soiteng, Nowgam, Rakhi Shalina, and Mehjoor Nagar. These places faced huge losses during the 2014 floods. The warnings were based on science and technical data. However, those in charge overlooked this warning, and, sadly, similar disasters have continued to occur since the 2014 floods The policymakers need to research and examine: Scientific dredging of the River Jhelum. Restoration of flood spill channels. Protection of wetlands. Elimination of encroachments. Reinforcement of bunds. Advanced flood forecasting systems. Kashmir’s Farmlands Are Disappearing Fast: What Can Be Done? In the last thirty years, Kashmir has changed quickly. Buildings are replacing fertile rice fields and orchards. The landscape that was once focused on farming now includes shopping centers, homes, roads, and schools. This fast loss of farmland affects food security, jobs, the environment, and the way Kashmiris live. Villages near Srinagar, Budgam, Pulwama, Baramulla, Anantnag, and Ganderbal are heavily affected. Some studies show that since the early 2000s, thousands of hectares of farmland have been converted to non-agricultural uses. In today's climate, strong agriculture is vital to regional strength. Constant land development weakens the Valley’s ability to adapt and makes both city and countryside residents more at risk during extreme weather. The environmental issues in Kashmir On August 14, 2025, Kishtwar in the Chenab Valley suffered a severe cloudburst. More than 67 people died, nearly 200 went missing, and 300 were injured. Another incident happened in the Kathua region. Why are cloudbursts happening so frequently, and what can we do about it? The Kashmir Himalayas are a fertile ground for cloudbursts. This happens because two weather systems affect the area. We get moisture from western disturbances and the southwest monsoon, which brings moisture from the Bay of Bengal and the Arabian Sea. When moisture reaches Kashmir, it gathers in heavy clouds. Strong winds quickly push this moisture up, reaching the Himalayas and forming dense clouds. After a while, these clouds become too heavy for the atmosphere to hold. When they can't support the weight anymore, they burst. This is called a cloudburst. It has recently happened in Kishtwar, Kathua, and Uttarakhand. We have stripped away all the trees in the forest. We are building big concrete structures, mining, cutting down trees, and changing the use of the land. This loose soil mixes with heavy rain, causing flash floods. These floods destroy everything in their path, including lives, buildings, and more. The study shows that the world is already feeling the effects of a warming planet. In Kashmir, this results in unpredictable rainfall. The area is changing from steady snowfall to sudden heavy rain, which the land cannot handle. This significantly increases the risk of severe flash floods and landslides, such as the disastrous floods that hit the valley in 2014. The region is getting warmer. In July 2024, Kashmir experienced an unusual heatwave, with record-high temperatures. This shows a shift towards subtropical heat in an area that usually has a temperate climate. Extreme weather events are increasing in number and severity. From 2010 to 2022, the region experienced over 2,800 such events, including heavy rains, flash floods, cloudbursts, and landslides, which caused major loss of life and property. What Has The Paris Agreement Achieved After 11 Years Of Action? More than a decade after the Paris Agreement was adopted in 2015, the global approach to climate change has changed. However, it still struggles to meet its main objectives. Eleven years after the important meeting in Paris, the results of the Paris Agreement are mixed. The agreement has helped prevent a harmful rise in temperatures, but it has also highlighted major political divides. This March, temperatures in Kashmir are hitting record highs usually seen in May. This unusual heat raises worries about climate change and its effects in the area, known for its beautiful winter scenery. As we reflect on a decade of commitments, we see a sad irony: the countries that contributed the least to climate change are suffering the most. These nations often bear the burden, paying for the emissions of wealthier countries through their own hardship and debt. (The Author is a Bio Consultant and can be reached at: ask@tahirmaqsood.com )

stories.headline: Scenario of Livestock and Agriculture in Pre and Post- Independent India: Introspection
stories.title: Scenario of Livestock and Agriculture in Pre and Post- Independent India: Introspection
stories.summary: Livestock and agriculture production is considered as the backbone of India’s economy and food security. Despite rapid industrialization, over 46% of India’s total workforce is engaged in agriculture and allied sectors, while roughly 60-65% of the population depends on it for their primary livelihood. However, these sectors have undergone an intense transformation since independence of India in 1947. Indian agriculture during pre- independence was characterized by traditional farming practices like using of tillers, sickles and manual labour with little or no mechanization which eventually resulted in low productivity. Livestock has traditionally complemented crop cultivation by providing a source of draught power, manure, milk and hence an additional household income. It also provided financial security to the families during periods of economic distress. Immediately after independence, India faced widespread poverty, low agricultural productivity and an urgent need to strengthen India’s economy. Following independence, agricultural research, irrigation facilities, improved seeds, fertilization and mechanization gradually transformed agricultural and livestock production. Over time, these initiatives contributed to major agricultural transformations commonly described as Green, White, Blue and Golden Revolutions. The history of livestock and agricultural development cannot be understood only through the increase in production. An introspective assessment must also examine who benefited from these developments, what environmental burdens accompanied them and whether leads to lasting prosperity for farmers and other livestock owners. Livestock and Agriculture during the Pre-independence Era Livestock formed an essential component of traditional farming system. Cattle and buffaloes served draught power while manure was used as a fertilizer for soil. Milk and its byproducts served as a household nutrition and also provided income. Indigenous breeds had valuable adaptive characteristics like tolerance to local climatic conditions and ability to survive under low input management systems. But, livestock productivity was restricted by insufficient nutrition, infectious diseases and parasitic infections. Treatment of animals in many rural areas depended on traditional knowledge and locally available traditional remedies and access to veterinary hospitals was limited. Dairy marketing was also unorganized and inadequate milk collection, chilling, processing and transportation facilities limited the commercial potential of livestock production. Limited availability of scientific support and organized infrastructure further restricted their capacity to improve production. During the pre-independence era, Indian agriculture was predominantly dependent on rainfall, local seeds and manual labour. Farming was primarily meeting the household food requirements and there was a limited access to modern agricultural machinery, irrigation and other scientific facilities. Due to inadequate irrigation, limited availability of good quality seeds and insufficient fertilizers, agricultural productivity was also low. Farmers were prone to droughts, floods and other natural calamities. Poor storage and transportation facilities further restricted the movement of agricultural production and increased post-harvest losses. Colonial land revenue system further contributed to unequal relationships between land-owners and cultivators. This practice often limited farmers’ ability to invest in irrigation, soil improvement and other long-term agricultural assets which ultimately lead to crop failure, disease outbreaks and other economic losses. Before the widespread expansion of monetized rural markets, barter and customary exchange arrangements played important roles in various village economies. Livestock and agricultural produce was exchanged for essential items and household goods. Sometimes, occupational groups used to receive a share of the produce and harvest in return for their services. These arrangements strengthened interdependence within rural communities but it also restricted economic exchange only to local networks and limit farmers’ bargaining power and accumulate savings. As commercial agriculture expanded, monetary transactions and regulated markets gradually became more important. Farmers gained more opportunities to sell their produce for money and purchase essential inputs like seeds, fertilizers, machinery etc. But this transition didn’t ensure fair returns to primary producers due to transportation cost, price fluctuation and inadequate storage. The historical transition from barter to organized agricultural marketing indicates an important economic change but it also reflects the need for transparent markets and profitable prices. Post-Independence Transformation: Revolution in Agriculture and Allied Sciences After independence, land reforms became an important element of India’s rural development strategy. The abolition of intermediary landholding systems, tenancy reforms and redistribution of surplus land were intended to minimize exploitation and the condition of cultivators. The principle of land to the tiller represented the idea that those who cultivate the land should enjoy greater security and receive a fairer share of benefits produced by their labour. However, its application varied from state to state. Incomplete land records, resistance from powerful landowners meant that landlessness and unequal access to productive resources persisted. Land fragmentation was the other major challenge. Population growth and subsequent division of agricultural holdings among generations contributed to smaller and more scattered landholdings. These conditions limited the use of machinery, irrigation investments, crop diversification and the economic viability of farming. The Green revolution, which was introduced during the mid-1960s, marked a significant transformation in Indian agriculture. Dr. M. S. body: However, these sectors have undergone an intense transformation since independence of India in 1947.

Indian agriculture during pre- independence was characterized by traditional farming practices like using of tillers, sickles and manual labour with little or no mechanization which eventually resulted in low productivity.
Livestock has traditionally complemented crop cultivation by providing a source of draught power, manure, milk and hence an additional household income.
It also provided financial security to the families during periods of economic distress.
Immediately after independence, India faced widespread poverty, low agricultural productivity and an urgent need to strengthen India’s economy.
Following independence, agricultural research, irrigation facilities, improved seeds, fertilization and mechanization gradually transformed agricultural and livestock production.
Over time, these initiatives contributed to major agricultural transformations commonly described as Green, White, Blue and Golden Revolutions.
The history of livestock and agricultural development cannot be understood only through the increase in production.

An introspective assessment must also examine who benefited from these developments, what environmental burdens accompanied them and whether leads to lasting prosperity for farmers and other livestock owners.
Livestock and Agriculture during the Pre-independence Era Livestock formed an essential component of traditional farming system.
Cattle and buffaloes served draught power while manure was used as a fertilizer for soil.
Milk and its byproducts served as a household nutrition and also provided income.
Indigenous breeds had valuable adaptive characteristics like tolerance to local climatic conditions and ability to survive under low input management systems.
But, livestock productivity was restricted by insufficient nutrition, infectious diseases and parasitic infections.
Treatment of animals in many rural areas depended on traditional knowledge and locally available traditional remedies and access to veterinary hospitals was limited.
Dairy marketing was also unorganized and inadequate milk collection, chilling, processing and transportation facilities limited the commercial potential of livestock production.
Limited availability of scientific support and organized infrastructure further restricted their capacity to improve production.
During the pre-independence era, Indian agriculture was predominantly dependent on rainfall, local seeds and manual labour.
Farming was primarily meeting the household food requirements and there was a limited access to modern agricultural machinery, irrigation and other scientific facilities.
Due to inadequate irrigation, limited availability of good quality seeds and insufficient fertilizers, agricultural productivity was also low.
Farmers were prone to droughts, floods and other natural calamities.
Poor storage and transportation facilities further restricted the movement of agricultural production and increased post-harvest losses.
Colonial land revenue system further contributed to unequal relationships between land-owners and cultivators.

This practice often limited farmers’ ability to invest in irrigation, soil improvement and other long-term agricultural assets which ultimately lead to crop failure, disease outbreaks and other economic losses.
Before the widespread expansion of monetized rural markets, barter and customary exchange arrangements played important roles in various village economies.
Livestock and agricultural produce was exchanged for essential items and household goods.
Sometimes, occupational groups used to receive a share of the produce and harvest in return for their services.
These arrangements strengthened interdependence within rural communities but it also restricted economic exchange only to local networks and limit farmers’ bargaining power and accumulate savings.
As commercial agriculture expanded, monetary transactions and regulated markets gradually became more important.

Farmers gained more opportunities to sell their produce for money and purchase essential inputs like seeds, fertilizers, machinery etc. But this transition didn’t ensure fair returns to primary producers due to transportation cost, price fluctuation and inadequate storage.
The historical transition from barter to organized agricultural marketing indicates an important economic change but it also reflects the need for transparent markets and profitable prices.
Post-Independence Transformation: Revolution in Agriculture and Allied Sciences.
After independence, land reforms became an important element of India’s rural development strategy.
The abolition of intermediary landholding systems, tenancy reforms and redistribution of surplus land were intended to minimize exploitation and the condition of cultivators.
The principle of land to the tiller represented the idea that those who cultivate the land should enjoy greater security and receive a fairer share of benefits produced by their labour.
However, its application varied from state to state.
Incomplete land records, resistance from powerful landowners meant that landlessness and unequal access to productive resources persisted.
Land fragmentation was the other major challenge.
Population growth and subsequent division of agricultural holdings among generations contributed to smaller and more scattered landholdings.
These conditions limited the use of machinery, irrigation investments, crop diversification and the economic viability of farming.
The Green revolution, which was introduced during the mid-1960s, marked a significant transformation in Indian agriculture.

Moreover indiscriminate crossbreeding without taking attention to nutrition and healthcare compromised animal welfare.

However, the expansion of fisheries created environmental concerns like water pollution, eutrophication, habitat destruction, disease outbreaks in intensive aquaculture and salanisation of agricultural land.

Modernization of livestock and agriculture production Beyond the major agricultural revolutions, the post-independence period witnessed considerable changes in farm inputs, machinery, animal breeding and livestock management.
High yielding seeds, chemical fertilizers, tractors, threshers, harvesters and irrigation equipment increased the production and reduced the time required for many farming operations.
Rural roads and the expansion of agricultural markets improved connectivity between producers and consumers.
At the time of independence in 1947, India did not have dedicated agricultural universities but only 17 agricultural or veterinary colleges affiliated with general universities.
Today, India has approximately 74 agricultural and allied universities recognized by the Indian Council of Agricultural Research (ICAR).
The ICAR Lab-to-Land Programme, launched in 1979, was specifically designed to transfer viable technologies from laboratories to farmers’ fields.

However, rising input costs, excessive fertiliser use, pesticide residues, machinery related expenses and the exclusion of resource-poor farmers from technology-intensive systems remain important concerns.
Industrialisation and urbanisation create additional pressures through pollution, waste generation and the conversion of agricultural land into non-agricultural uses.
Road connectivity has also influenced agricultural development.

But farmers in many remote areas experienced high transportation costs, inadequate storage facilities and limited processing opportunities.
Better connectivity must therefore be complemented by transparent marketing, reliable procurement, storage facility and opportunities for value addition.
Currently, India possesses one of the world’s largest livestock populations and is also the world’s largest milk producer, reflecting the importance of livestock in its agricultural economy.
Livestock development benefited from genetic improvement, artificial insemination, improved nutrition, vaccination, disease diagnosis and reproductive management.
Crossbreeding of indigenous cattle with exotic dairy breeds contributed to increased milk production in many production systems.
Improved management of indigenous breeds and the conservation of locally adapted genetic resources also became increasingly important.
Timely diagnosis of diseases, access to qualified veterinary professionals and responsible use of medicines remain essential for sustainable livestock development.
In livestock sector also, the benefits didn’t reach all livestock owners equally and there was also shortage of veterinary services, inadequate fodder and insufficient infrastructure.
Poor manure management can contribute to water contamination and inadequate waste disposal and unsuitable housing can affect animal health.

Conclusion.
The transition in scenario of livestock and agriculture from pre-independence era to post-independence era of India represents a major transformation in livestock and agricultural production.
